name: Megiddo
description: Strategic city controlling the Jezreel Valley pass on the Via Maris trade route. 25+ layers of occupation make it one of the most excavated sites in the world.
significance: UNESCO World Heritage Site; site of the Battle of Megiddo (1457 BCE); later gave its name to Armageddon

paperLinks.title: The Megiddo Expedition — Tel Aviv University

name: Hazor
description: The largest Canaanite city in the Late Bronze Age, with a population of 20,000-40,000. Joshua burned it. Solomon later rebuilt it as a royal city. Destroyed by Assyrians in 732 BCE.
significance: Head of all Canaanite kingdoms (Josh 11:10); Amarna letters document its kings; UNESCO World Heritage Site

paperLinks.title: Hazor Excavation Project — Hebrew University of Jerusalem

youtubeLinks.title: Tel Hazor — Israel's Largest Biblical City

name: Lachish
description: Judah's second most important city after Jerusalem. The Lachish Letters (586 BCE) are among the oldest Hebrew documents. Famous Assyrian reliefs in the British Museum depict Sennacherib's siege.
significance: Key Judean fortress; Lachish reliefs in British Museum; Lachish Letters document final days of First Temple period

youtubeLinks.title: The Siege of Lachish — Sennacherib's Reliefs

name: Gezer
description: Important city at the crossroads of the coastal plain and Shephelah. The Gezer Calendar (10th c. BCE) is one of the oldest Hebrew inscriptions. Egyptian pharaoh burned Gezer and gave it as dowry to Solomon.
significance: Gezer Calendar (earliest Hebrew agricultural inscription); strategic crossroads site; built by Solomon (1 Kgs 9:15-17)

name: Shechem
description: Central highland city where Abraham built his first altar in Canaan. Jacob bought land and dug a well here. Joshua held the covenant renewal ceremony at Shechem. Rehoboam was crowned here before the kingdom split.
significance: First site where God appeared to Abraham in Canaan; place of covenant renewal; Jeroboam made it northern capital

name: Arad
description: Excavations revealed a remarkable Israelite temple at Arad — one of only two known Israelite temples from the biblical period. Contains altars of the same dimensions as described in the Torah. The Arad ostraca (600+ Hebrew inscriptions) document military administration.
significance: One of two known Israelite temples (with Moza); Arad ostraca are largest collection of pre-exilic Hebrew inscriptions

name: Beersheba
description: Southernmost city of biblical Israel ('from Dan to Beersheba'). Abraham dug a well and planted a tamarisk tree here. Isaac built an altar. Elijah fled here from Jezebel. A dismantled Iron Age altar was found, possibly from Hezekiah's reforms.
significance: Marks southern extent of biblical Israel; Abraham's covenant with Abimelech (Gen 21); UNESCO World Heritage Site

paperLinks.title: Tel Beer-Sheba — UNESCO World Heritage Site

name: Tel Dan
description: Northernmost city of biblical Israel. The Tel Dan Stele (9th century BCE) contains the earliest extra-biblical reference to the 'House of David.' Jeroboam erected a golden calf shrine here. The city controlled a major spring feeding the Jordan River.
significance: Tel Dan Stele — first extra-biblical mention of 'House of David'; Jeroboam's golden calf shrine (1 Kgs 12:29)

name: City of David
description: The original settlement of Jerusalem on the southeastern ridge south of the Temple Mount. David conquered it from the Jebusites around 1000 BCE. Hezekiah's Tunnel (701 BCE) is still walkable — cut through solid rock to secure water supply during Sennacherib's siege.
significance: David's capital; Hezekiah's Tunnel; Siloam Inscription; Pool of Siloam; ongoing excavations reveal 3000+ years of occupation

paperLinks.title: City of David Archaeological Park — Official Site

youtubeLinks.title: City of David: Archaeological Discoveries in Jerusalem

name: Babylon
description: One of the ancient world's greatest cities. Under Nebuchadnezzar II, Babylon was rebuilt with massive walls, the Ishtar Gate, the ziggurat Etemenanki (possibly the Tower of Babel prototype), and legendary Hanging Gardens. The Jewish exile was centered here.
significance: Tower of Babel tradition; site of Jewish exile; Ishtar Gate now in Berlin's Pergamon Museum; UNESCO World Heritage Site

paperLinks.title: The Babylon Project — Oriental Institute, Chicago

name: Ur of the Chaldees
description: A major Sumerian city-state near the mouth of the Euphrates. The Royal Cemetery of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) contained extraordinary gold artifacts. The massive ziggurat of Ur-Nammu still stands. This is the city where Terah took his family before Abraham's call.
significance: Abraham's hometown (Gen 11:28-31); Royal Cemetery of Ur with spectacular gold artifacts; well-preserved ziggurat

paperLinks.title: Ur in Iraq — Penn Museum Excavations

youtubeLinks.title: Ur of the Chaldees — The Royal Cemetery

name: Eridu
description: Considered the world's first city according to the Sumerian King List. Continuously occupied from 5400 BCE, Eridu has 18 layers of temple construction. The Sumerian flood story was preserved here. Possibly the origin of the Garden of Eden traditions.
significance: Possibly world's oldest city; 18 superimposed temples; source of Sumerian flood narrative; near ancient Persian Gulf coastline

name: Uruk
description: The world's first true city (c. 3200 BCE), with a population of 50,000-80,000. Uruk gave us the first writing (cuneiform), the first monumental architecture, and complex administration. The Epic of Gilgamesh's hero ruled here. Genesis lists it among Nimrod's cities.
significance: First true city; birthplace of writing; Epic of Gilgamesh; biblical 'Erech' (Gen 10:10)

name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)
description: Major Late Bronze Age city-state on the Syrian coast. Excavations since 1929 revealed a palace library with thousands of clay tablets in Ugaritic — closely related to Hebrew. The Baal Cycle and other myths illuminate the Canaanite religious world confronted by the biblical prophets.
significance: Ugaritic language closest to biblical Hebrew; Baal Cycle illuminates Canaanite religion; destroyed c. 1185 BCE

name: Persepolis
description: The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, built by Darius I and Xerxes. Its massive terrace held palaces, audience halls (apadanas), and treasury storehouses. Delegations from all 23 satrapies brought tribute — depicted in famous carved reliefs. Burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE.
significance: Persian imperial capital; reliefs show delegations from all provinces; Xerxes (Ahasuerus of Esther) built the famous harem here

youtubeLinks.title: Persepolis — Capital of the Persian Empire

name: Tell el-Amarna (Akhetaten)
description: Akhenaten's purpose-built capital for his monotheistic Aten religion, founded c. 1346 BCE and abandoned after his death. The Amarna Letters archive — 382 clay tablets — documents diplomatic correspondence between Egypt and Canaanite city-states, Mitanni, Babylon, Assyria, and Hatti.
significance: Amarna Letters document Late Bronze Age international diplomacy; first experiment in state monotheism; abandoned within 20 years

name: Ekron
description: One of the five Philistine cities. The Ark of the Covenant was brought here after being taken from Israel. The largest olive oil industrial center of the ancient Near East was discovered here — 115 olive oil presses from the 7th century BCE. A royal dedicatory inscription confirmed the identification.
significance: Ark of the Covenant brought here (1 Sam 5); largest ancient olive oil factory; royal inscription confirms identification

name: Ashdod
description: One of the five Philistine cities and the largest. The Ark of the Covenant was housed in the temple of Dagon here after capture. Excavations revealed continuous occupation from Bronze Age through Byzantine period. The idol of Dagon fell before the Ark twice.
significance: Ark captured and placed in Dagon's temple (1 Sam 5); Dagon's idol falls twice before the Ark; major Philistine city

name: Shiloh
description: The central sanctuary of Israel during the period of the Judges — home of the Tabernacle and Ark of the Covenant for approximately 300 years. Hannah prayed here for a son; Samuel grew up here. Destroyed by Philistines around 1050 BCE.
significance: Home of the Tabernacle and Ark (Josh 18); Samuel's childhood home; Hannah's prayer (1 Sam 1); destroyed before Jerusalem Temple

paperLinks.title: Shiloh: Where the Tabernacle Came to Rest (Associates for Biblical Research)

youtubeLinks.title: Excavating Biblical Shiloh — The Tabernacle Site

name: Hebron
description: The cave of Machpelah purchased by Abraham from Ephron the Hittite became the burial place of the patriarchs and matriarchs. David's first capital before Jerusalem. The tomb structure above Machpelah was built by Herod the Great and stands today.
significance: Cave of Machpelah — burial of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Sarah, Rebekah, Leah; David's first capital (2 Sam 2:11)

name: Mizpah
description: Central assembly point for Israel in Judges and Samuel. Samuel held his circuit court here. After Jerusalem's fall in 586 BCE, Mizpah became the administrative capital of the Babylonian province of Judah under Gedaliah.
significance: Samuel anoints Saul near here (1 Sam 10); Gedaliah's provincial capital after Jerusalem's fall (2 Kgs 25:23-25)

name: Elephantine
description: Island in the Nile where a Jewish military garrison maintained a temple to YHWH in the 5th century BCE. The Elephantine Papyri (discovered 1893) contain letters, contracts, and religious documents from this Jewish community — remarkable evidence of diaspora Judaism during the Persian period.
significance: Jewish temple to YHWH outside Jerusalem; Elephantine Papyri document 5th century BCE Jewish diaspora in Egypt

name: Tell es-Sakan (ancient Gaza)
description: The ancient tell underlying modern Gaza, with continuous occupation since at least the Early Bronze Age. Egyptian pharaohs maintained garrisons and administrative centers here. The Philistine city of Gaza controlled the southern coastal trade route. Samson met his end in the temple of Dagon here.
significance: Samson's death at the Philistine temple (Judg 16); major Egyptian administrative center; gateway to Sinai

name: Tel Dan Stele Site
description: The site where, in 1993-94, three fragments of an Aramaic stele were discovered mentioning 'the House of David' — the first extra-biblical reference to the Davidic dynasty. The stele was likely erected by Hazael of Damascus after defeating Israelite and Judahite forces.
significance: Tel Dan Stele — first extra-biblical proof of David's dynasty; erected by Hazael of Aram c. 835 BCE
